  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as 
<br class="ltx_break">Satisfiability Modulo Theory</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Hyunseok Oh<sup id="id1" class="ltx_sup">*</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sam Stern<sup id="id2" class="ltx_sup">†</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Youngki Lee<sup id="id3" class="ltx_sup">*</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Matthai Philipose<sup id="id4" class="ltx_sup">‡</sup>
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><sup id="id5" class="ltx_sup">*</sup>Seoul National University
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname"><sup id="id6" class="ltx_sup">†</sup>U. Mass. Amherst
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname"><sup id="id7" class="ltx_sup">‡</sup>Microsoft
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Natural language understanding requires interleaving textual and logical reasoning, yet large language models often fail to perform such reasoning reliably. Existing neurosymbolic systems combine LLMs with solvers but remain limited to fully formalizable tasks such as math or program synthesis, leaving natural documents with only partial logical structure unaddressed. We introduce Logitext, a neurosymbolic language that represents documents as natural language text constraints (NLTCs), making partial logical structure explicit. We develop an algorithm that integrates LLM-based constraint evaluation with satisfiability modulo theory (SMT) solving, enabling joint textual-logical reasoning. Experiments on a new content moderation benchmark, together with LegalBench and Super-NaturalInstructions, show that Logitext improves both accuracy and coverage. This work is the first that treats LLM-based reasoning as an SMT theory, extending neurosymbolic methods beyond fully formalizable domains.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models (LLMs) remain unreliable at logical reasoning in natural language, often producing inconsistent or incomplete results despite recent progress <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sakai et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. (2025)</a></cite>. Logical solvers provide reliable guarantees but are confined to fully formalizable domains such as math and program synthesis. Existing neurosymbolic systems combine LLMs with logical solvers to achieve strong results in these domains <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olausson et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wen et al. (2025)</a></cite>, but they face two key limitations. First, they remain restricted to fully formalizable settings and thus cannot naturally handle documents that mix textual and logical structure. Second, they typically adopt a staged architecture in which the LLM formalizes the problem once and the logical solver executes it. This design precludes the iterative interleaving of textual and logical reasoning required for many natural language tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Real-world documents highlight this gap. Policies specify conditions on user posts, instructions impose formatting rules, and statutes constrain legal interpretations. These constraints are seldom fully formalizable, yet they combine naturally with logical operators and interact with calculations. To capture such cases, we introduce <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Logitext</span>, a neurosymbolic language that expresses constraints directly in text. At the core of Logitext are <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">natural language text constraints (NLTCs)</span>, a representation that makes partial logical structure explicit and allows textual and symbolic constraints to work together.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Example.</span> Consider a policy stating that “a post must be removed if it is both hateful and an immediate threat.” The textual notions of “hateful” and “immediate threat” cannot be fully formalized in logic, but they can be represented as NLTCs. Logitext links these textual constraints with a logical conjunction, ensuring that the decision depends on both the logical structure and the outcome of the textual judgments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We realize this idea by extending satisfiability modulo theory (SMT) with a new theory for textual constraints. Modern SMT logical solvers assign values to variables step by step and propagate the consequences across theories such as strings, floats, and sets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Davis et al. (1962)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marques-Silva and Sakallah (1999)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">de Moura and Bjørner (2008)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Barrett et al. (2010)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al. (2017)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rümmer and Wahl (2010)</a></cite>. With NLTCs, this propagation requires solving textual constraints iteratively so that assignments remain consistent with Boolean conditions. We develop a theory that performs this process efficiently and integrate it into existing SMT solvers, thereby positioning LLM-based reasoning as an SMT-solver-compatible theory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contributions.</span> This paper formalizes LLM-based reasoning as an SMT theory and introduces the first framework to support SMT-solver-compatible reasoning with partial logical structure:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Concept:</span> We show the necessity of interleaving textual and logical reasoning and characterize the limitations of staged approaches (§<a href="#S2" title="2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Language:</span> We introduce Logitext, a neurosymbolic language that enriches documents with logic and represents them as NLTCs interfacing with SMT solvers (§<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 The Logitext language ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, §<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">NLTC Solver:</span> We present an algorithm that solves NLTCs and extends the SMT framework with this capability (§<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation:</span> We show that Logitext outperforms staged baselines on a new content moderation benchmark and improves accuracy and coverage on LegalBench and Super-NaturalInstructions (§<a href="#S4" title="4 Evaluation ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We illustrate the need for interleaved textual and logical reasoning using a content moderation policy.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text</h3>

<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<figure id="S2.F1.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S2.F1.sf1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="430.37" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 430.37" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,430.37) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 424.46 C 0 427.73 2.64 430.37 5.91 430.37 L 544.09 430.37 C 547.36 430.37 550 427.73 550 424.46 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 424.46 C 1.97 426.64 3.73 428.4 5.91 428.4 L 544.09 428.4 C 546.27 428.4 548.03 426.64 548.03 424.46 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 17.24)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:28.86em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.25em;font-size:10pt;" height="402.82" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 399.36)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">

<span id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<span id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Bias: </span><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:6.5pt;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">C</mi><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{3}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">Message contains stereotyping, insensitive remarks, fear of difference, non-inclusive language, microaggressions, justifying biases by seeking out like-minded people, accepting negative or misinformation/screening out positive information.</span></span>

<span id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Violence: </span><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:6.5pt;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">C</mi><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">4</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{4}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">Message is related to murder, rape, assault, arson, terrorism, vandalism, desecration, or threats.</span></span>
</span></span>
<span id="S2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="S2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Genocide: </span><span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:6.5pt;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><math id="S2.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">C</mi><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{5}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">Message is related to the act or intent to deliberately and systematically annihilate an entire people.</span></span>
</span></span>
</span>
<span id="S2.F1.sf1.pic1.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.F1.sf1.pic1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Based on the above, a message is an immediate threat if <span id="S2.F1.sf1.pic1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:6.5pt;"><math id="S2.F1.sf1.pic1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">C</mi><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">6</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{6}</annotation></semantics></math></span> <span id="S2.F1.sf1.pic1.1.2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">it expresses a violent or genocidal intention and the context is enough to suggest that the safety and/or life of an individual or group of people is at risk</span>.</span></span>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span></figcaption>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Example: A content moderation policy (a) illustrates a fine-grained mix of logical and textual constraints. Combined with (b), it yields a prompt that requires compositional logical reasoning, and with (c-d), combinatorial reasoning.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows a common LLM use case. A policy document (Figure <a href="#S2.F1.sf1" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(a)</span></a>) defines notions such as “disruptive behavior” and “immediate threat.” When paired with a task description (Figures <a href="#S2.F1.sf2" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(b)</span></a>–<a href="#S2.F1.sf4" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(d)</span></a>) and an input message, the document becomes an LLM prompt whose <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">reliable reasoning</span> is the objective.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The document expresses intent through both textual and logical relations. <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">Shaded</span> text <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">within</span> each clause <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> specifies its <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">meaning</span> relative to the input message <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> and possibly other clauses. For example, given <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=</annotation></semantics></math> “Americans love ice cream,” clause <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> (“addressed at a group”) and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (“targeted by nationality”) both evaluate to True. Text <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">between</span> clauses then constrains these meanings logically. Whether a message is disruptive (<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>) may now be written as:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=C_{1}\land C_{2}\land(C_{3}\lor C_{4}\lor C_{5})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>∧</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>∧</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>∨</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>∨</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=C_{1}\land C_{2}\land(C_{3}\lor C_{4}\lor C_{5})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compositional reasoning.</span> The classification task in Figure <a href="#S2.F1.sf2" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(b)</span></a> asks whether a message is disruptive (<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>) or an immediate threat (<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>). Solving for <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> requires one pass of textual reasoning to evaluate each <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, followed by logical evaluation of the formula. At first glance, <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> appears to need only textual reasoning (<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{6}</annotation></semantics></math>). However, <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{6}</annotation></semantics></math> checks whether the message “expresses violent or genocidal intention,” which depends on prior results <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{4}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{5}</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> requires information from a logical disjunction <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{4}\lor C_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>∨</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{4}\lor C_{5}</annotation></semantics></math>, showing the benefit of interleaving logical with textual reasoning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Combinatorial reasoning.</span> The constrained generation task in Figure <a href="#S2.F1.sf3" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(c)</span></a> reverses the classification problem: instead of labeling a given message, the goal is to generate a message <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> that satisfies both a partial assignment of clause values and the policy as a whole. This requires two steps. First, a logical solver proposes candidate assignments for the relevant clauses (e.g., <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{1}\ldots C_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{1}\ldots C_{5}</annotation></semantics></math>) that are consistent with the partial assignment and with the logical definition of <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>. Second, a generator synthesizes a message <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> whose text realizes those clause assignments. If the synthesis step fails to produce a valid message, the process must repeat with a new candidate assignment. The high-coverage generation task in Figure <a href="#S2.F1.sf4" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(d)</span></a> is an even harder variant: it requires generating messages that realize many or all satisfying assignments, not just one. Such tasks inherently demand iterative cooperation between logical solving and textual synthesis.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Logical reasoning gaps</h3>

<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F2.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18095v1/comp-gap.svg" id="S2.F2.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/350;" width="548" height="350"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span>Compositional gap</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F2.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18095v1/results_plot_combi_gap_v6.svg" id="S2.F2.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/330;" width="548" height="330"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(b) </span>Combinatorial gap</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Gaps in logical reasoning (see App. <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Definitions of gaps ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>) on content moderation across LLMs.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How well do LLMs perform the logical reasoning needed for these tasks? To evaluate this, we define <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">reasoning gaps</span>: the difference between (1) performance when an LLM handles textual reasoning and a logical solver executes logical reasoning, versus (2) performance when the LLM alone handles the entire prompt. We denote the reasoning gap for compositional problems <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> and that for combinatorial problems by <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>, as defined in App. <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Definitions of gaps ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>. Our dataset contains five content safety policies with 6–21 clauses.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S2.F2.sf1" title="In Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 Logical reasoning gaps ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(a)</span></a> shows <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> across models, measured as classification accuracy. Smaller models exhibit large compositional gaps, while stronger models narrow them. Within each model, the size of the gap increases with task complexity, reflecting the number of interacting clauses.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S2.F3.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="817.57" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 817.57" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,817.57) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 811.67 C 0 814.93 2.64 817.57 5.91 817.57 L 544.09 817.57 C 547.36 817.57 550 814.93 550 811.67 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 811.67 C 1.97 813.84 3.73 815.61 5.91 815.61 L 544.09 815.61 C 546.27 815.61 548.03 813.84 548.03 811.67 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 13.78)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:57.1em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="790.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 790.03)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S2.F3.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:36.62em;">
<span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">```<span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">(M:str, d, t, C1, C2, C3, C4, C5, C6, C7)</span>```
<br class="ltx_break">Messages containing disruptive behavior are those {{let <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C1</span> = [[addressed at a group (excludes messages targeted at just an individual)]] where "messages" is <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M</span>}}
and {{let <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C2</span> = [[the group targeted by the message is defined by {{forsome [[ethnicity]], [[gender]], [[color]], [[nationality]], [[sexual orientation]], [[race]], or [[physical disability]] }}]] where "message" is <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M</span>}},
and the message matches at least one of the following sub-rules:

<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">Bias: {{let <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C3</span> = [[Message contains stereotyping, insensitive remarks, fear of difference, non-inclusive language, microaggressions, justifying biases by seeking out like-minded people, accepting negative or misinformation/screening out positive information.]] where "message" is <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M</span>}}

<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">Violence: {{let <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C4</span> = [[Message is related to murder, rape, assault, arson, terrorism, vandalism, desecration, or threats.]] where "message" is <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M</span>}}

<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">Genocide: {{let <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C5</span> = [[Message is related to the act or intent to deliberately and systematically annihilate an entire people.]] where "message" is <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M</span>}}

<br class="ltx_break">```
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C8 = C4 or C5
<br class="ltx_break"></span>```
<br class="ltx_break">Based on the above, a message is an immediate threat if {{let <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C6</span> = [[it expresses a violent or genocidal intention]] where "it expresses a violent or genocidal intention" is <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C8</span>}} and {{let <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C7</span> = [[the context is enough to suggest that the safety and/or life of an individual or group of people is at risk.]] where "the context" is <span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.16" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M</span> }} 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">```
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.17" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">d = C1 and C2 and (C3 or C4 or C5)</span> 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S2.F3.pic1.1.1.1.18" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">t = C6 and C7</span> 
<br class="ltx_break">```</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Content moderation policy example implemented as Logitext Document</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S2.F2.sf2" title="In Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 Logical reasoning gaps ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(b)</span></a> shows <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> for combinatorial reasoning, measured as the number of distinct correct assignments generated. Here the gaps are dramatic: even state-of-the-art models such as GPT-5 fail to recover over 99% of satisfying assignments that an SMT solver (Z3) can enumerate, and GPT-4o-mini fails completely across all tasks. Unlike compositional gaps, which shrinks with model scale, combinatorial gaps remain severe even for frontier models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, although improvements in models gradually address compositional gaps, combinatorial gaps (which affect the solve/synthesize loop of language reasoning) are still significant. Logitext is designed to bridge these gaps by helping specify textual vs logical intent of natural documents precisely, and finely interleave LLM decoding and logic solving to support combinatorially efficient and semantically faithful interpretation of the intent.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Logitext: Language, representation and solver</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a conventional textual prompt as in Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we convert it to Logitext program format by annotating it (Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 The Logitext language ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>). The Logitext program is <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">parsed</span> into a set of hybrid <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Natural Language Text Constraints</span> (NLTCs) (Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>). Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a> presents an LLM-based solver NLSolver for NLTCs and pairs it with a logical solver to produce the final task response.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>The Logitext language</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Logitext extends conventional text prompts into <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">hybrid text/logic documents</em>, enabling natural language clauses to interact directly with formal constraints. It supports <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">partial formalization</em>: only those parts of a document that benefit from logical structure are annotated, while the rest remain textual. This selective annotation allows reasoning to interleave between textual interpretation and logical propagation, as motivated in Section <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A Logitext document (Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.2 Logical reasoning gaps ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) enriches a textual policy (Figure <a href="#S2.F1.sf1" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(a)</span></a>) with four constructs (see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Syntax for Logitext documents ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a> for the full syntax):</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Variable declarations</span> (e.g., <span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">(M:str, d, t, …)</span>) define the symbols that participate in logical constraints. Variables may be Boolean or string; string variables must be typed explicitly (e.g., <span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M:str</span> for an input message).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Textual let bindings</span> of the form <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{{let &lt;var_0&gt; = [[&lt;clause&gt;]] where &lt;subclause_1&gt; is &lt;var_1&gt; ... and &lt;subclause_n&gt; is &lt;var_n&gt;}}</span> (a) binds a textual clause (i.e., a sentence fragment) to a logical variable (for example, the clause “addressed at a group …just an individual” is named <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C1</span>), and (b) associates sub-clauses within the clause (e.g., “messages”) with external variables, e.g. <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M</span>. Intuitively, <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;clause&gt;</span> represent a constraint between the variables <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;var_i&gt;</span>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Logical constraint blocks</span> (delimited by <span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">```</span>) specify logical relations (e.g., <span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">t = C6 and C7</span>) among variables, using <span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">pyz3</span> notation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">de Moura and Bjørner (2008)</a></cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Convenience constructs</span> such as <span id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">forall</span> and <span id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">forsome</span> compactly handle textual lists, internally expanded into disjunctions or conjunctions over let-bindings.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Such Logitext documents are “executed” using a <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">check()</span> function as in constraint solving. Given a partial assignment <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">p</span> of variables in a document <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">d</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">check(d, p, cover)</span> searches for a satisfying assignment that respects both the logical and textual constraints:</p>
<blockquote id="S3.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">check(d:LogitextDocument, p:Dict[str, bool|str], cover:Option[bool]) -&gt; Dict[str, bool|str] | unsat | timeout</span></p>
</blockquote>
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.3" class="ltx_p">If a solution exists, <span id="S3.SS1.p3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">check()</span> returns a full assignment as a mapping from variable names to values. Otherwise it reports unsatisfiability or timeout. With the optional flag <span id="S3.SS1.p3.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cover</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.p3.3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">check()</span> enumerates multiple satisfying assignments. This mechanism generalizes the familiar <span id="S3.SS1.p3.3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">complete()</span> execution of text prompts to a richer constraint-satisfaction setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The expressiveness of Logitext unifies diverse language understanding tasks under a single interface. The three tasks of Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(b)–(d) are expressed uniformly as constraint checking: (i) <span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">classification</span> (<span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">lt.check(d, {’M’: M})[’d’]</span>), (ii) <span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">partially constrained instance generation</span> (<span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">lt.check(d, {’C4’: False, ’C5’: False})[’M’]</span>), and (iii) <span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">coverage generation</span> (<span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">[g[’M’] for g in lt.check(d, {’C4’: False, ’C5’: False}, cover=True)]</span>). In contrast to raw prompting, Logitext makes explicit the logical structure of documents, enabling solver-style propagation to cooperate with LLM-based textual reasoning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Natural language text constraints</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The constructs in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 The Logitext language ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a> define how Logitext documents combine textual clauses with logical constraints. To reason with such documents, we require a representation that treats textual clauses as first-class objects alongside logical formulas. We introduce <em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">natural language text constraints (NLTCs)</em>, which bind clauses to variables, record references to external context, and allow seamless interaction with solvers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recall from the previous section that, in addition to a variable declaration section, an unparsed Logitext document <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> consists of alternating code blocks and text blocks (Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.2 Logical reasoning gaps ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). Each code block is a sequence of logical strings <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, e.g., <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C8 = C4 or C5</span>. Each text block contains a sequence of let-binding text strings <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> of the form:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{let }v=[[c]]\textbf{ where }u_{1}\textbf{ is }p_{1}\ldots u_{n}\textbf{ is }p_{n}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">let </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold"> where </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold"> is </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold"> is </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{let }v=[[c]]\textbf{ where }u_{1}\textbf{ is }p_{1}\ldots u_{n}\textbf{ is }p_{n}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> is a boolean variable to which <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> is bound, while the <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are strings (typically substrings of <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>) associated with variables <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> defined elsewhere.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To process a document <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>, we parse it into an abstract representation <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> in three steps:</p>
<ol id="S3.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Variable collection.</span> Identify boolean variables <math id="S3.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="vs_{D}=v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">vs_{D}=v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> and string variables <math id="S3.I2.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="us_{D}=u_{1},\ldots,u_{n^{\prime}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">us_{D}=u_{1},\ldots,u_{n^{\prime}}</annotation></semantics></math>. These variables include those declared explicitly and those introduced in let bindings as above.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Logical constraint parsing.</span> Convert each logical string <math id="S3.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> from a logical text string into a solver-ready formula <math id="S3.I2.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> using Z3’s parser.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Textual constraint parsing.</span> Translate each let-binding <math id="S3.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> into an NLTC <math id="S3.I2.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\nu=(v,c,\{u_{1}:p_{1},\ldots,u_{n}:p_{n}\},d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu=(v,c,\{u_{1}:p_{1},\ldots,u_{n}:p_{n}\},d)</annotation></semantics></math>: each NLTC binds <math id="S3.I2.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> to the clause <math id="S3.I2.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, records its dependencies, and points to the full document <math id="S3.I2.i3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> so <math id="S3.I2.i3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> can be interpreted in context.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">After parsing, the abstract document is <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=(vs_{D},us_{D},\phi_{D},\nu_{D})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=(vs_{D},us_{D},\phi_{D},\nu_{D})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{D}=\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{D}=\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> are logical constraints and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu_{D}=\nu_{1},\ldots,\nu_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ν</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu_{D}=\nu_{1},\ldots,\nu_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> are NLTCs. Reasoning proceeds with respect to a partial assignment <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{D}:us_{D}\cup vs_{D}\rightarrow\text{bool}|\text{str}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow><mo>∪</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mtext>bool</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo fence="false">|</mo><mtext>str</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{D}:us_{D}\cup vs_{D}\rightarrow\text{bool}|\text{str}</annotation></semantics></math>, which specifies known variable values and lets the solver–LLM loop infer the rest, as discussed in the next section.</p>
</div>
</section>

                     <math id="alg1.l6a.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{sat}\leftarrow\text{false}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>sat</mtext><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mtext>false</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{sat}\leftarrow\text{false}</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l6a.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">;</span> <math id="alg1.l6a.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\pi}\leftarrow\bar{\pi}\cup\{\nu_{k}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>π</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>π</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>∪</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\pi}\leftarrow\bar{\pi}\cup\{\nu_{k}\}</annotation></semantics></math>
     

</div>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l8a" class="ltx_listingline">

                  <math id="alg1.l8a.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u^{*}\leftarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>u</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u^{*}\leftarrow</annotation></semantics></math> LLMPropose(<math id="alg1.l8a.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="alg1.l8a.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="alg1.l8a.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>π</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="alg1.l8a.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>u</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>)<span id="alg1.l8a.2" class="ltx_text" style="float:right;"><math id="alg1.l8a.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\triangleright" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊳</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\triangleright</annotation></semantics></math> Refine 
</span>
</div>
