</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Core Logitext constraint solving algorithms</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows how Logitext solves hybrid systems of natural language text constraints (NLTCs, <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math>) and logical constraints (<math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>), given shared Boolean variables <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="vs" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">vs</annotation></semantics></math>, text-string variables <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="us" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">us</annotation></semantics></math>, and a partial assignment <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{D}</annotation></semantics></math> of Booleans and strings. The goal is to extend <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{D}</annotation></semantics></math> into a complete satisfying assignment <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{\prime}_{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>π</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{\prime}_{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, using an LLM-based solver as an extension to the core logical (aka SMT) solver.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The overall strategy is simple. A logical solver (we use <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z3</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">de Moura and Bjørner (2008)</a></cite>) produces candidate Boolean assignments that satisfy Boolean constraints (Fig <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>a), and our LLM-based solver (called NLSolver) then attempts to produce assignments to string variables that satisfy text constraints while maintaining the Boolean assignments (Fig <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>a).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We begin with the outer logical solver loop of Fig <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>a. We use <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z3</annotation></semantics></math> to generate candidate assignments <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>Z</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> of variables <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="vs" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">vs</annotation></semantics></math> consistent with <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{D}</annotation></semantics></math> (Line <a href="#alg1.l2" title="In Algorithm 1 ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). We now loop sequentially over unbound string variables <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> (Lines <a href="#alg1.l4" title="In Algorithm 1 ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>-<a href="#alg1.l9" title="In Algorithm 1 ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>), trying to find satisfying assignments for each, compatible with all assignments so far. Each <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> is passed to text-constraint solver NLSolver, which attempts to generate a text string value <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>u</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> for each unbound string variable <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> (Line <a href="#alg1.l5" title="In Algorithm 1 ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>), given the constraints <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu[u]\subseteq\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>⊆</mo><mi>ν</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu[u]\subseteq\nu</annotation></semantics></math> that read or write <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math>, and the assignments so far (<math id="S3.SS3.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{s}\cup\pi_{D}\cup\pi_{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>Z</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{s}\cup\pi_{D}\cup\pi_{Z}</annotation></semantics></math>). If NLSolver fails to find a <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>u</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, we block <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z3</annotation></semantics></math> from regenerating candidate assignment <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>Z</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{Z}</annotation></semantics></math>, break out of the loop over <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="us" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">us</annotation></semantics></math> (Line <a href="#alg1.l6" title="In Algorithm 1 ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>) and continue generating more candidate Boolean assignments (Lines <a href="#alg1.l8" title="In Algorithm 1 ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, <a href="#alg1.l2" title="In Algorithm 1 ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). If all string variables <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> are assigned, we declare success and return all assignments accumulated (Lines <a href="#alg1.l7" title="In Algorithm 1 ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, <a href="#alg1.l9" title="In Algorithm 1 ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>). If no candidates remain, we declare unsatisfiability (Line <a href="#alg1.l3" title="In Algorithm 1 ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">NLSolver (Fig <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>b) is given a variable <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math>, a set <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math> of NLTCs that read <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math>, and a partial assignment <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>. Its job is to produce a textual string <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>u</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> that satisfies constraints <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math> given partial assignment <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>. It does so through a propose-verify-refine loop. It starts by prompting an LLM, via the LLMPropose() call (see Appendix <a href="#alg3" title="Algorithm 3 ‣ A.5.2 LLMPropose algorithm details ‣ A.5 Solver algorithms ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), to propose a candidate <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>u</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> that satisfies <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> (Line <a href="#alg1.l1a" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). It then uses <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> rounds (Line <a href="#alg1.l2a" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) to refine this solution to one that satisfies <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math>. In each round, for every NLTC <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu_{k}\in\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>ν</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu_{k}\in\nu</annotation></semantics></math>, it calls into an LLM via LLMVerify() (Appendix <a href="#alg4" title="Algorithm 4 ‣ A.5.3 LLMVerify algorithm details ‣ A.5 Solver algorithms ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) to infer the truth value for the variable bound by <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, given <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u=u^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>u</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u=u^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> and existing assignment <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, and compares this truth value to that required by the partial assignment <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> (Line <a href="#alg1.l5a" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). If all truth values are compatible, it returns <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>u</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> as a satisfying assignment (Line <a href="#alg1.l7a" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>). Otherwise, it uses LLMPropose() to refine <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>u</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> (Line <a href="#alg1.l8a" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>). The refinement is guided by an additional “needs-to-change” set <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>π</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math>, which lists the constraints that <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>u</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> currently violates. After <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> rounds of not finding <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>u</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, we declare failure (Line <a href="#alg1.l9a" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The above describes the essence of how Logitext solves NLTCs. In practice, we include two further techniques that have modest impact. First, note that LLMPropose() may produce a piece of text that does not match the current partial assignment <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, and is therefore rejected by LLMVerify(). However, LLMPropose() itself may be called many thousands of times for various candidate assignments in the check() algorithm. Given that calls to LLMPropose() are relatively expensive since it calls out to LLMs, we cache results from these calls and consider them for use on future calls to NLSolver. Second, when we propose a refinement of textual value <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>u</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, it helps not only to have the “needs-to-change” list mentioned above, but also a history of the previous refinements proposed on <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>u</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> and their outcome from LLMVerify. These two techniques are described further in the appendix, and the (modest but noticeable) impact of caching is analyzed in the evaluation section (Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.1 Benchmarks and setup ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<figure id="S3.F5.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18095v1/taskwise_plot_partial.svg" id="S3.F5.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/177;" width="548" height="177"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span>Text instance generation (TIG)</figcaption>

<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Evaluation</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Benchmarks and setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Content Moderation (CMOD).</span> A new benchmark of five multi-page moderation policies (2–5 pages, 6–22 annotated clauses) covering drugs (22 clauses), politics (8), religion (6), bullying (21), and fraud (12) (see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS9" title="A.9 Content moderation dataset example ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.9</span></a> for an example). These tasks are designed to reflect realistic compliance settings where policy documents constrain user-generated content.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Legal Benchmark (LegalBench, LB).</span> We select five tasks from LegalBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guha et al. (2023)</a></cite>, an extensive benchmark for reasoning over statutory and regulatory text. The tasks cover domains such as diversity jurisdiction, housing and warranty law, and supply-chain transparency. Each task is 20–50 lines with 2–4 annotated clauses. This benchmark captures challenges in legal text where precise logical structure interacts with natural language.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Natural Instructions (SNI).</span> We select five tasks from Super-NaturalInstructions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2022)</a></cite>, focusing on problems with implicit logical constraints such as detecting grammatical inconsistencies, reasoning about hypothetical actions, and identifying abusive content. Each task is 3–10 lines with 2–5 annotated clauses. This benchmark tests generalization to diverse instruction-following tasks beyond policy or law.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Together these benchmarks yield 15 tasks with 10+ instances each, spanning policy, legal, and open-domain instructions. All tasks require mapping text inputs to structured outputs (classifications or constrained generations). We evaluate Logitext on three settings aligned with Fig. <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>:
(a) <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task execution (TE)</span> — measuring classification accuracy on task instances,
(b) <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Text instance generation (TIG)</span> — testing the ability to generate valid inputs under partial constraints, and
(c) <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Text coverage generation (TCG)</span> — enumerating as many valid inputs as possible.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F6.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18095v1/success_rate_plot_coverage_multimodel_fancy.svg" id="S4.F6.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/309;" width="548" height="309"></object>

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Text instance generation (TIG).</span>
Figure <a href="#S3.F5.sf1" title="In Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5(a)</span></a> compares Logitext with direct prompting.
With both GPT5 and GPT5-nano as base models, Logitext generates valid assignments reliably via <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">check()</span>.
The results indicate that (i) Logitext attains near-saturation performance even with the weaker GPT5-nano, while direct prompting to GPT5 shows noticeable degradation; and (ii) degradation is most evident on complex CMOD policies, although performance on Drugs is relatively stronger than other cases.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span>Candidate generation</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F7.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18095v1/coverage_latency_comparison_plot.svg" id="S4.F7.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/266;" width="548" height="266"></object>

</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Text coverage generation (TCG).</span>
Figure <a href="#S3.F5.sf2" title="In Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 Solving natural language text constraints ‣ 3 Logitext: Language, representation and solver ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5(b)</span></a> (log scale) reports coverage under a fixed time budget of 3000s.
Baseline GPT is allowed up to 5 iterations for candidate generation and 5 additional iterations for finding satisfying assignments.
Logitext achieves broader coverage, particularly with GPT5-nano.
Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> provides an explanation: candidate generation is significantly faster with Logitext since it uses a solver rather than repeated LLM calls (Fig. <a href="#S4.F7.sf1" title="In Figure 7 ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7(a)</span></a>).
The advantage is reduced in the solving phase (Fig. <a href="#S4.F7.sf2" title="In Figure 7 ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7(b)</span></a>), where NLSolver calls dominate, but this bottleneck is smaller for faster base models such as GPT5-nano.
We also report the LLM call statistics of NLSolver in Appendix Figure <a href="#A1.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ A.6 Number of LLM calls from NLSolver ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">NLSolver iterative refinement.</span>
Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.1 Benchmarks and setup ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows that NLSolver improves success rates as the number of iterations increases.
Caching can be beneficial in some settings (e.g., coverage generation with GPT5), though its overall effect across tasks is limited.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F8" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task Execution (TE).</span>
Figure <a href="#S4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>(left) presents accuracy on TE tasks using GPT-4o.
In addition to few-shot prompting, we include a neurosymbolic prompt that generates and executes code.
Logitext performs better on CMOD and NI benchmarks but underperforms on LegalBench.
Figure <a href="#S4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>(right) highlights two main sources of error:
(i) in some cases, clause-level outputs <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[[C_{i}]]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[[C_{i}]]</annotation></semantics></math> were incorrectly predicted by the LLM, but the LLM-only approach produced correct answers using holistic reasoning, revealing a robustness limitation for Logitext;
(ii) in other cases, lists such as “x, y, and z” were intended as examples rather than conjuncts, but were annotated as the latter.
These issues point to the need for clause-level error correction and more careful handling of list annotations in future work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, the experiments show that Logitext improves performance on both constrained generation and classification tasks across multiple benchmarks, while highlighting remaining challenges in clause-level robustness and annotation handling.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Related work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompt-based reasoning.</span>
Prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2022)</a></cite> and Tree-of-Thought (ToT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al. (2023)</a></cite> elicit multi-step reasoning by decomposing queries into textual steps. Chain-of-Logic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Servantez et al. (2024)</a></cite> separates logical reasoning from answer prediction, aiming to improve consistency in step-wise deduction. While these approaches enhance local coherence or allow limited backtracking, they lack mechanisms to bridge deeper compositional and combinatorial reasoning gaps and cannot ensure global logical consistency across clauses. Once an error propagates, there is no principled way to validate against constraints. Our framework differs by explicitly defining these reasoning gaps and incorporating symbolic validation into the reasoning process itself.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Systematic generalization and constraint solving.</span>
Our challenges relate closely to systematic generalization tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lake and Baroni (2018)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Keysers et al. (2020)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim and Linzen (2020)</a></cite>, which demonstrate that sequence models fail when compositional rules must be recombined in novel ways. Similar issues arise in program synthesis and constraint satisfaction tasks, where LLMs can propose candidate programs or assignments (e.g., Codex for SAT/SMT) but collapse under combinatorial growth in the search space. These methods provide no principled mechanism to enforce or recover from violated constraints. We formalize these compositional and combinatorial reasoning gaps as structural limitations of LLM inference and show how solver integration can systematically mitigate them in natural language contexts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reasoning models.</span>
Reasoning models such as OpenAI o3/o4-mini and DeepSeek-R1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al. (2025)</a></cite> have shown improved performance on benchmarks for logical reasoning and robust instruction following. RL allows limited correction through feedback <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kalyanpur et al. (2024)</a></cite> or exploration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al. (2025)</a></cite>. However, they depend heavily on reward shaping or sample filtering, and lack a formal representational layer for partial logical structures. As a result, they cannot enforce symbolic constraints or recover from violated ones during inference. Our framework complements these advances by introducing a neurosymbolic language that supports constraint-aware reasoning within an SMT framework.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Neuro-symbolic reasoning.</span>
Recent systems such as LINQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olausson et al. (2023)</a></cite>, CLOVER <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ryu et al. (2025)</a></cite>, and ZebraLogic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. (2025)</a></cite> connect LLMs with symbolic solvers by translating natural language into executable logic programs. These approaches achieve strong guarantees when tasks are fully formalizable, but their reliance on complete logical structure restricts applicability to natural documents like policies or legal texts, where only fragments of logic are explicit. ZebraLogic also provided an initial study of the <span id="S5.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">combinatorial gap</span>, but its scope was limited to well-defined mathematical domains. In contrast, our work addresses this challenge in natural language contexts that inherently contain uncertainty and partial structure. We introduce natural language text constraints (NLTCs), enabling partial formalization and iterative solver-guided reasoning that better reflects the complexity of real-world documents.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work we introduced Logitext, a neurosymbolic framework that treats LLM reasoning as an SMT theory through natural language text constraints. We first motivated the need for such a framework by showing that even frontier LLMs continue to exhibit two reasoning gaps: compositional gaps that narrow with scale but persist, and combinatorial gaps that remain severe. By interleaving solver propagation with LLM decoding, Logitext provides a principled way to reduce these gaps. More broadly, our results suggest a path toward positioning LLMs as solver-compatible theories, opening opportunities for scalable, reliable, and trustworthy natural language reasoning.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Definitions of gaps</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each policy <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> is annotated with clauses <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and associated with a formula <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> as in Fig <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and Eqn<a href="#S2.E1" title="In 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, and comes with 10-20 test messages <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> each with ground truth <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmnameddefinition1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_nameddefinition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmnameddefinition1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 1</span></span><span id="Thmnameddefinition1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(<span id="Thmnameddefinition1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compositional gap <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{mp}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{mp}</annotation></semantics></math> of LLM <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> on prompt <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></h6>
<div id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, prompt <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> for (i) the meanings <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math> of clauses <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> , and (ii) whole-prompt result <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>. This results in overall accuracy <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a=\text{mean}_{j}\delta(h_{j},H_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mtext>mean</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a=\text{mean}_{j}\delta(h_{j},H_{j})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta(x,x^{\prime})=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta(x,x^{\prime})=1</annotation></semantics></math> if <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=x^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=x^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>, else <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>. Now, use a logical solver to evaluate <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}_{j}=\phi(b_{ij})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}_{j}=\phi(b_{ij})</annotation></semantics></math>, giving corresponding accuracy <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>. Then compositional gap <math id="Thmnameddefinition1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{mp}=a-a^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{mp}=a-a^{*}</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="Thmnameddefinition2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_nameddefinition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmnameddefinition2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 2</span></span><span id="Thmnameddefinition2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(<span id="Thmnameddefinition2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Combinatorial gap <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta^{\prime}_{mp}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta^{\prime}_{mp}</annotation></semantics></math> of model LLM <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> on prompt <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></h6>
<div id="Thmnameddefinition2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmnameddefinition2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prompt <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> to produce (i) all policy inputs <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, and (ii) complete assignments <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math> for clauses <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> such that the policy is true. Use a logical solver to filter out <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math> that do not satisfy <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>, and also to generate independently its satisfying assignments <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b^{*}_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b^{*}_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> (resp. <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n^{*}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n^{*}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>) be number of such assignments . The combinatorial gap is the relative discrepancy between these numbers: <math id="Thmnameddefinition2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta^{\prime}_{mp}=\text{mean}_{j}(n^{*}_{j}-n_{j})/n^{*}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mtext>mean</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta^{\prime}_{mp}=\text{mean}_{j}(n^{*}_{j}-n_{j})/n^{*}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>
</div>
</div>
</section>

</table>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Comparison of dataset instance counts and runs in the original submission vs. resubmission.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have expanded the dataset evaluated to 100 samples per task from 12 samples per task as shown in Table <a href="#A1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ A.3 Expanded dataset ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. We are in the process of running evaluations on the data. So far, we have completed full re-evaluation on 100 samples on 5 tasks (from Legalbench), partial re-evaluation on 50 samples (from Super-NaturalInstructions, SNI), and have not yet started re-evaluation on our most favorable dataset CMOD. For Legalbench and SNI, each task had sufficient samples that we were able to simply incorporate more samples from the existing dataset. For CMOD, we had to generate samples analogous to production moderation data, a task that requires some care.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We focused on re-running the Task Execution (TE) experiments (Figure <a href="#S4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>), both because these are the least favorable to us, and because the combinatorial gap experiments take much longer to run. Of course, we will complete running all experiments on all datasets over the next few days.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As Tables <a href="#A1.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ A.3 Expanded dataset ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and <a href="#A1.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ A.3 Expanded dataset ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> show, the expanded results don’t change the highest level message on the Task Execution task qualitatively: Logitext does provide a noticeable boost on many tasks, and prevails in 7 of 10 tasks, but the baseline model does do better in some cases. Perhaps interestingly, Logitext now does relatively better on Legalbench, prevailing in 4/5 tasks, and slightly worse on SNI (3/5). Once again, when Logitext fails, the main culprit seems to be clause-level evaluation errors, which we have discussed in more detail in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS4" title="A.4 Clause-level error analysis ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4</span></a>, and mentioned in the original submission.</p>
</div>

<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.4 </span>Clause-level error analysis</h3>

<figure id="A1.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18095v1/figs/heatmap.jpg" id="A1.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/386;" width="548" height="386" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>Clause-level accuracy for Disruptive Behavior policy from Figure <a href="#S2.F1.sf1" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(a)</span></a> </figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A1.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ A.4 Clause-level error analysis ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> is a quick analysis of clause-level accuracy for the “Disruptive Behavior” prompt of Figure <a href="#S2.F1.sf1" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Compositional vs combinatorial reasoning in natural text ‣ 2 Interleaved text/logic reasoning in text understanding ‣ Neurosymbolic Language Reasoning as Satisfiability Modulo Theory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(a)</span></a>. The x-axis of the figure lists the various clauses in the prompt<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            Note in the version of the example used in the body of the paper, we omit the Discrimination and Humiliation categories for brevity but they are included in this analysis, which was performed on the complete version of the policy document.</span></span></span>. The y-axis represents individual messages input to the prompt. Each message was run 100 times through the prompt using <span id="A1.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4.1-nano</span> as the base model. Each entry in the table is the fraction of times the answer for a particular clause was correct for that message. Some entries are missing because some runs did not complete.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Several points are worth noting, all admittedly only in the context of the current prompt:</p>
<ol id="A1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Sub-clause level inference can be quite stable across runs. They are usually either always correct or always wrong, only occasionally are they not 0 or 1. Thus the worst case of several sub-clauses at a time unpredictably producing errors due to stochastic variation is not inevitable.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Inference results are predominantly correct, i.e., sub-clause level accuracy may be much higher than “holistic” document-level accuracy.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Certain clauses (i.e., columns, e.g. Gender) are consistently interpreted incorrectly across inputs. In a production setting, we would consider re-wording these, hopefully yielding consistently <span id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">correct</span> clauses.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Most inputs (i.e., rows) always have at least one sub-clause evaluated incorrectly. This may seem fatal, until we recall the logic of the prompt is essentially
<math id="A1.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=\text{isGroup}\land\textbf{(}\text{PhysicalDisability}\lor\text{Color}\lor\text{Ethnicity}\lor\text{Gender}\lor\text{Nationality}\lor\text{Race}\lor\text{SexualOrientation}\textbf{)}\land\textbf{(}\text{Bias}\lor\text{Discrimination}\lor\text{Humiliation}\lor\text{Genocide}\lor\text{Violence}\textbf{)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>isGroup</mtext><mo>∧</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">(</mtext><mtext>PhysicalDisability</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo>∨</mo><mtext>Color</mtext><mo>∨</mo><mtext>Ethnicity</mtext><mo>∨</mo><mtext>Gender</mtext><mo>∨</mo><mtext>Nationality</mtext><mo>∨</mo><mtext>Race</mtext><mo>∨</mo><mrow><mtext>SexualOrientation</mtext><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">)</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo>∧</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">(</mtext><mtext>Bias</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo>∨</mo><mtext>Discrimination</mtext><mo>∨</mo><mtext>Humiliation</mtext><mo>∨</mo><mtext>Genocide</mtext><mo>∨</mo><mrow><mtext>Violence</mtext><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">)</mtext></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=\text{isGroup}\land\textbf{(}\text{PhysicalDisability}\lor\text{Color}\lor\text{Ethnicity}\lor\text{Gender}\lor\text{Nationality}\lor\text{Race}\lor\text{SexualOrientation}\textbf{)}\land\textbf{(}\text{Bias}\lor\text{Discrimination}\lor\text{Humiliation}\lor\text{Genocide}\lor\text{Violence}\textbf{)}</annotation></semantics></math>. If a clause Gender, which is supposed to be False by default, wrongly evaluates to True, it will not cause an end-to-end error given that Gender is part of a larger disjunction (“or”) operation. Thus the precise value of the error, the operation it is part of, and the values of other operands in the operation all contribute to whether a higher-level error is generated. Clausal error does not necessarily imply global error.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">While this analysis is by no means comprehensive, it gives some intuition of why the introduction of clause-level errors does not necessarily lead to catastrophic failure at the whole-formula level.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.5 </span>Solver algorithms</h3>

The version includes details of caching and history, as mentioned in the main body of the paper.</p>
</div>

<div id="alg4.l4" class="ltx_listingline">
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">4:</span>

<section id="A1.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.8 </span>LLM Prompts used for Neurosymbolic approach</h3>

<div id="A1.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">These are the LLM prompts for the neurosymbolic approach used in Task Execution (TE) experiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Decide what level of reasoning is needed for a task,
then route to the appropriate reasoning prompt</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Routing level 1: LLM-heavy simple decision with minimal Z3 validation</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS8.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Routing level 2: Boolean logic breakdown with moderate Z3 reasoning</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS8.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Routing level 3: Complex constraints with heavy Z3 reasoning</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg5" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 5</span> </span> Neurosymbolic algorithm</figcaption>
<div id="alg5.4" class="ltx_listing ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom ltx_listing">
<div id="alg5.l1" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">1:</span>
              
              
            <span id="alg5.l1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input:</span> Task description

</div>
<div id="alg5.l2" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">2:</span>
              
              
            <span id="alg5.l2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Output:</span> True/False

</div>
